content: I am designing and building PetalProgress: a habit-tracking app built around mandala visualization, where each check-in adds to the mandala design.

The project started from a specific observation: most habit apps are designed for the version of the user who doesn't need them, built for perfect days, with mechanics that punish the reality of being human.
PetalProgress is an attempt to build something different. This case study is about the decisions that shaped it, and the research and reasoning behind each one.
I researched why existing habit apps produce poor outcomes. The data is striking: research suggests up to 90% of users abandon habit-tracking apps within 30 days.
Across app store reviews, Reddit communities, and published studies, five pain points emerged consistently. Each one is a design problem, not a user motivation problem.

A Cohorty analysis of 6,000+ users found that heavily gamified apps retain only 23% of users at 90 days, compared to 53% for simple check-in apps. More telling: gamified app users who stopped using the app maintained their habits only 11% of the time at six months, versus 41% for non-gamified users. The tool undermined the goal.

Building a habit still requires showing up. PetalProgress does not change that. What it tries to remove are the design barriers that make tracking and promoting habit formation harder than it needs to be.
/petalprogress-diagram-01.png
alt: Diagram mapping five common habit app pain points to PetalProgress design solutions

content: Traditional mandala creation is meditative. An artist returns to the piece session by session, layer by layer. No single mark makes or breaks the work; what matters is the practice of returning to it.
A finished mandala is a record of every session the artist showed up for. A missed day is not a flaw. It is simply a day the artist was elsewhere.
PetalProgress replaces the streak counter with a mandala: a visualization that shows what you built, not what you missed.
/petalprogress-mandala-editor-poc.png
alt: Proof of concept for the PetalProgress mandala editor showing petals added through check-ins

content.header: Decision 01: Weekly Targets, Not Daily Mandates
content: Research finding: rigid daily scheduling is one of the most emotionally harmful design patterns in habit apps. A Habitify user put it precisely: "I'd love the ability to track a habit over a week. Trying to force them to a specific day makes me less likely to do them."
The decision: PetalProgress uses weekly targets. Users set how many times per week they want to check in, not which specific days. Missing Tuesday is not a failure if Wednesday still happens.
The tradeoff: weekly targets are slightly harder to visualize than daily streaks. By adding shapes to the pattern, the mandala design can address that issue with additional layers.
Research finding: the act of logging becomes its own burden. One writer described it precisely: "I made a Daily specifically for checking and updating Habitica", a habit for the habit tracker.
The design goal was to get check-in time under 30 seconds without opening the app. The solution: email-based check-in. A single reply to a daily email logs the habit.

Free users get email tracking assigned to their first mandala from day one. When that mandala completes, tracking auto-transfers to the next active mandala. Users can reassign it manually at any time. Petal+ unlocks email tracking across all mandalas simultaneously.
/petalprogress-diagram-02.png
alt: Diagram showing the email-based check-in flow and how email tracking transfers between mandalas

content.header: Decision 03: A Genuinely Useful Free Tier
content: Research finding: apps that advertise as free and immediately gate core features generate significant negative sentiment and drive app-switching. One reviewer called it "almost unusable without subscription."
The decision: the free tier should constitute a complete habit practice, not a trial. Three active mandalas, all themes, full check-in history and gallery, email tracking on the first mandala.

The line between free and paid is about depth, not access. Petal+ at $1.99/month unlocks unlimited mandalas, email tracking on all of them, reminders, calendar view, and 20% off the shop (one print order covers a month).
/petalprogress-diagram-03.png
alt: Diagram comparing the free tier and Petal+ subscription features

content: Research finding: the most common failure pattern isn't lack of willpower. It's that users set up 10-15 ambitious habits at onboarding, sustain them for a week, and collapse entirely. The enthusiastic setup creates the conditions for failure.
The decision: PetalProgress onboards users with weekly mandalas only. Longer timeframes (monthly, quarterly, yearly) exist in the product, but are not introduced at setup.
A completed weekly mandala is achievable. That completion creates the motivation to start another. Longer timeframes become meaningful once the habit has actually formed.
/petalprogress-diagram-04.png
alt: Diagram illustrating the progression from weekly mandalas to longer timeframes as habits form

content: A completed mandala is not just a data visualization: it is a record of a practice. I wanted to explore what it would mean to take that record off the screen.

Before the shop, there is sharing. When a user completes a mandala, they can generate a shareable image for social media: a free, built-in engagement feature that turns individual progress into something visible. It is one of the few habit app mechanics that doesn't ask anything of the user; the mandala is already beautiful, and sharing it is optional.

Social traction creates a natural funnel: someone sees a completed mandala, recognizes what it represents, and downloads the app. This is an organic acquisition path that most habit apps don't have, because their outputs aren't worth sharing.

The shop extends this logic into the physical world. Users can order their completed mandala as an art print, magnet, or button: a proof of concept for what that layer could look like. The object becomes a tangible marker of the habit they built.
/petalprogress-shop-poc.png
alt: Proof of concept for the PetalProgress shop showing completed mandalas as printable art products

content: The individual product works because it feels personal, not managed. The Teams product had to preserve that experience for members while giving coaches and program managers what they actually need.

Members have the same experience as any individual user: their mandala grows the same way. The coach layer adds habit assignment, an engagement dashboard, and at-risk alerts. The member never sees themselves as a data point.

The end-of-program artifact is where the two layers converge: printed mandalas for every member. For a gym or wellness program, that is something tangible to hand someone at the end of 12 weeks. It marks the work they did.
/petalprogress-diagram-05.png
alt: Diagram showing the Teams product structure with coach dashboard and member mandala experience

content: PetalProgress started as a spark, the kind artists describe when an idea arrives and simply has to be followed. The concept felt right before the research confirmed it, and the research confirmed it.

The user data validates the core visual: momentum-based tracking outperforms streaks, flexible scheduling outperforms rigid daily grids, and simple tools build more durable habits than complex ones. The mandala is not just an aesthetic choice; it is the right structure for the problem.
I am building this because I believe I see it. That is a different starting point than most habit apps, and I hope it shows in the decisions.
